newsitem.title: USA: Progressive sees 1997 profit margins down.
newsitem.headline: Progressive sees 1997 profit margins down.

text.p: Progressive Corp said it expects profit margins to decrease in 1997 as it increases spending in a move to add new customers faster.
Progressive said it expects its combined ratio to move toward 96 percent in 1997, up from 90.9 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996.
A Progressive spokesman declined to say exactly how high the combined ratio might go, but said "If you're a betting person, don't bet it will stay as low as it is."

The combined ratio indicates whether a company is earning a profit on the business it writes. An underwriting profit occurs when the ratio is below 100 percent and the profit increases as the combined ratio decreases.
But, Progressive said, "Growing the number of policyholders builds intrinsic value because renewals, particularly of standard and preferred risks, are more profitable than first year business."
Progressive said it has adjusted its 1997 bonus, or gainsharing, program to encourage agents to write more standard and preferred risks.
"The drive to add customers faster will result in more spending to promote our brand and to develop more claim adjusters and customer service representatives," Progressive said.
"These costs, along with expected losses on first year business, are likely to bring profit margins more in line with our four percent objective," Progressive said.
Progressive declined to estimate the costs associated with the move to add new customers.
However, Merrill Lynch analyst Jay Cohen said he expects only about a 1.5 point deterioration in Progressive's combined ratio, which would cost the company about $50 million.
For 1996, Progressive's combined ratio was 91.5 percent compared with 94.3 percent in 1995.
"I see it as an investment," Cohen said. "Yes, it will cost them something this year in the margin; that's the investment. But they set themselves up to grow earnings in 1998 and beyond," he said.
